Triggers.value: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible

Threat.value: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I can't deal with even the slightest upset

vignette: Meera was seven when the masked intruders smashed through the door of the family flat, their boots crunching over shattered glass and the sharp tang of spilled antiseptic from a torn medical kit. She spent those childhood years hiding beneath a heavy quilt, learning to associate sudden silences with impending violence. At seventy-nine, those same sensory anchors still pierce her composure. When the airline cabin crew sprays disinfectant near her galley station, her breath catches. Certain old playback melodies on the terminal radio halt her in her tracks. Even now, she cannot bring herself to sleep alone or in an unfamiliar hotel room, the quiet amplifying the ghost of those initial heavy footsteps. These sudden sensory cues immediately throw her nervous system into overdrive, directly fueling a state of persistent threat. She wakes during the night to check whether she is safe, pacing the hallway until her joints ache, and remains alert at home, feeling on guard even inside her own residence. The sustained physiological arousal spills into irritability, manifesting as angry outbursts when her husband, Arjun, asks a simple question. Because the triggers constantly signal danger, she has come to believe she is a lousy coper, convinced she cannot deal with even the slightest upset without completely unraveling. What frightens her most is the certainty that she can't rely on herself to keep her family safe. Because the triggers constantly signal danger, she instinctively turns to maladaptive strategies to escape the distress. She delays sleep, staying up until very late just to outrun the quiet hours, and overeats to manage distress, pulling on comfort foods until her stomach protests. In private, she indulges revenge fantasies, imagining getting revenge on the people responsible as a mental escape from her perceived powerlessness. Her negative appraisals directly fracture her recall, leaving her with only fragmented pieces that do not fit together, while the maladaptive avoidance directly fractures her memories further. The negative appraisals also amplify her threat response, ensuring the hypervigilance never truly subsides. The vivid quality of these memories dictates her present-day reality. A certain song on the terminal radio does not merely remind her of the past; the more real than normal intensity of the recall forces her nervous system to register the present moment as equally dangerous, directly amplifying her trigger sensitivity. Because the memories feel like they are happening right now, they directly heighten her threat monitoring, making her wake during the night to check whether she is safe and intensifying her irritability. The fragmented pieces actively feed back into her negative appraisals, confirming to her that she is a bad coper. The relentless reliving of the event also drives her maladaptive strategies, as the sheer weight of the imagery pushes her to delay sleep and overeat just to numb the cognitive load. Her persistent threat state directly sharpens her trigger sensitivity, ensuring that the hospital smell or a familiar melody immediately sparks a panic response. Her compensatory behaviors now form an inescapable loop. The constant alert at home and her irritability directly push her toward delaying sleep and overeating, as the physiological arousal becomes too exhausting to tolerate. That same hypervigilance fragments her memories further, ensuring that only disconnected pieces remain, while simultaneously hardening her negative appraisals into a fixed belief that she cannot rely on herself. Even her strategies reinforce the original cues, as avoiding rest keeps her nerves frayed and highly reactive to the very smells and melodies she tries to ignore. The maladaptive avoidance also sustains her threat response, keeping her on guard long after the intruders are gone. Her career as an airline pilot demanded precision, yet the galley now feels like a pressure cooker where antiseptic clouds and distant musical echoes threaten to ground her. She has started taking long, unnecessary layovers, avoiding the crew lounge when the cleaning staff arrives with their chemical sprays. She sought help last month after a routine pre-flight briefing, her hands shaking as she reached for her headset, realizing the avoidance had finally outpaced her ability to navigate a simple checklist. Meera hopes a clinician might untangle the knot she has carried for sixty years, though she remains terrified that the past will never stop dictating the safety of her present.
